etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English muscle, muscule, muskylle, and in part from Middle French muscle, from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”, literally “little mouse”) because of the mouselike appearance of some muscles, from mūs (“mouse”). Doublet of mussel. More at mouse.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A contractile form of tissue which animals use to effect movement.

quote.citation: 1701, Nehemiah Grew, “Of the Use of Organized Bodies”, in Cosmologia Sacra: Or A Discourse of the Universe as It is the Creature and Kingdom of God. […], London:  […]  W[illiam] Rogers, S[amuel] Smith, and B[enjamin] Walford: […], →OCLC, 1st book, paragraph 18, page 27:
quote.text: For as the Trunk of the Body, is kept from tilting forvvard by the Muſcules of the Back: So, from falling backvvard, by theſe of the Belly.

definitions.definition: (countable) An organ composed of muscle tissue.

quote.citation: 1912 January, Zane Grey, chapter VIII, in Riders of the Purple Sage […], New York, N.Y., London: Harper & Brothers Publishers, →OCLC:
quote.text: His brow and hair and the palms of his hands were wet, and there was a kind of nervous contraction of his muscles. They seemed to ripple and string tense.

quote.citation: 1943 November – 1944 February (date written; published 1945 August 17), George Orwell [pseudonym; Eric Arthur Blair], Animal Farm […], London: Secker & Warburg, published May 1962, →OCLC:
quote.text: You, Boxer, the very day that those great muscles of yours lose their power, Jones will sell you to the knacker  […]

definitions.definition: (uncountable, usually in the plural) A well-developed physique, in which the muscles are enlarged from exercise.

quote.citation: 2008, Lou Schuler, "Foreward", in Nate Green, Built for Show, page xii
quote.text: The fact that I was middle-aged, bald, married, and raising girls instead of chasing them didn't really bother me. Muscles are cool at any age.

quote.text: The lesson to be drawn from the events of 1914, to Roosevelt's mind, was that civilization needed muscle to defend it, not just solemn words.

quote.citation: 2013, John D. MacDonald, The Long Lavender Look, page 15:
quote.text: It was going to take muscle to pluck Miss Agnes out of the canal.

quote.text: How can the unions - or more specifically the RMT—possibly think this is a good time to exert a bit of industrial muscle and indulge in strikes both on the national railway and the London Underground?

quote.citation: 1985, Lance Parkin, The Infinity Doctors, page 34:
quote.text: It was easy enough to dodge him, let him crash into the floorboards. Peltroc knew that his priority was the leader, not the hired muscle.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To use force to make progress, especially physical force.

quote.text: Nothing the Nebraskans ever again recorded managed to muscle more than minimal attention.

quote.text: "Here!" I passed out stacks of money. T.C. hadn't had time to batch it up, so some of it was just laying loose in money bags and I passed all that shit out to Rome while Pimp muscled Miss Lady around.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move forcefully or with great strength.
